$comment: lenses.json — the three wrongness dimensions. Source: paper p.3–8 + the dimensions/examples table (credit-scoring running example). Structure per user review 2026-10-29: shared positive baseline, per-lens baseline rationale, negative examples (collapsible).

positiveBaseline.title: Positive baseline
positiveBaseline.explanation: The loan applicant was denied because their income is low and debt-to-income ratio is high, exceeding the default risk threshold.
positiveBaseline.context: Running example: an AI-based credit scoring system.

lenses.name: Coherence
lenses.tooltip: The explanation is logically consistent with itself — no contradictions inside.
lenses.definition: Whether the explanation maintains a consistent and logical internal structure. A lack of coherence means the internal structure is logically conflicting, contradictory, or structurally impossible — independent of whether premises and conclusions are valid.
lenses.baselineWhy: The explanation forms a logically consistent syllogism. It would be coherent even if the premises were false and the applicant would have repaid their loan.

goodExample.explanation: “You rated ‘Interstellar’ 5 stars, and both films are directed by Christopher Nolan.”
goodExample.why: Coherent even if you end up not enjoying “Inception” — the internal logic holds.

flawedExample.setup: A credit-scoring model explains its decision for one applicant.
flawedExample.explanation: “Higher income boosted the creditworthiness score (+30) and dropped it (−20) — for the exact same instance.”
flawedExample.why: The explanation contradicts itself: the same feature cannot simultaneously raise and lower the score. This is incoherence.

facets.name: Rule contradiction
facets.example: A rule-based explainer justifies the rejection with mutually exclusive conditions (“income < $30k and income > $80k”).

facets.name: Counterfactual contradiction
facets.example: A counterfactual explanation requires the applicant to simultaneously increase and decrease their requested loan amount.

facets.name: Stochastic instability
facets.example: A stochastic local feature attribution method reports income simultaneously boosts (+30) and lowers (−20) credit score across runs.

facets.name: Non-sequitur examples
facets.example: An example-based method justifies the rejection using similarities with three images from a conflicting class (“accepted”).

facets.name: Semantic non-sequitur
facets.example: An LLM-generated explanation for the rejection states: “Your loan has been approved because our evaluation shows severe insolvency and a high probability of imminent default.”

lenses.footnote: An explanation is already incoherent if it corresponds to a single facet. It can — but does not need to — correspond to multiple facets.

lenses.name: Validity
lenses.tooltip: The explanation matches the real-world facts — what is actually true.
lenses.definition: Whether the explanation aligns with the real-world ground truth the model seeks to reflect — both the factual premises and the ground-truth outcomes. A lack of validity means the explanation asserts factually incorrect claims and/or misrepresents actual patterns or causal relations.
lenses.baselineWhy: The explanation is only valid given that the data is correct, these features predict empirically observable real-world default risk, and the applicant would have defaulted. It would still be valid if this is not the logic the model actually applied.

goodExample.setup: An email filter correctly flags a message as spam.
goodExample.explanation: “Flagged because it was sent from an unknown sender, contains 12 suspicious links, and asks for your banking passwords.”
goodExample.why: Every claim matches the real-world facts of the message.

flawedExample.setup: A weather forecast correctly predicts rain today.
flawedExample.explanation: “Rain is expected because of low humidity.”
flawedExample.why: The prediction is right, but the stated cause is factually wrong — an invalid premise.

facets.name: Invalid feature values
facets.example: A local attribution-based method reports a bank balance of $0, when the applicant's real-world balance is $50,000.

facets.name: Invalid target label
facets.example: Any explanation plausibly justifies acceptance of the applicant even though the applicant will default.

facets.name: Spurious proxies
facets.example: A local attribution-based method reports the applicant's zip code as a primary reason for rejection, even though zip code is only a demographic proxy for race rather than a causal driver of creditworthiness.

facets.name: Invalid counterfactual
facets.example: A counterfactual explanation suggests to increase income by $300, but the applicant would default even with this profile.

lenses.footnote: An explanation is already invalid if it corresponds to a single facet. It can — but does not need to — correspond to multiple facets.

lenses.name: Faithfulness
lenses.tooltip: The explanation reflects how the model actually processed the input.
lenses.definition: How well the explanation represents the true internal reasoning and mechanics of the AI model. A lack of faithfulness means the explanation is misaligned with how the model actually processed the input to reach its prediction.
lenses.baselineWhy: The explanation is only faithful if income and debt-to-income ratio were actually the primary factors driving the classification. It would still be faithful if the applicant would have repaid their loan.

goodExample.setup: A spam filter assigns 90% of its internal risk weight to the phrase “claim your free prize now”.
goodExample.explanation: The feature attribution reports “claim your free prize now” as the top factor driving the spam classification.
goodExample.why: The reported driver matches the model's actual internal weighting.

flawedExample.setup: A CV-screening model internally uses zip code as a proxy for race to reject an applicant.
flawedExample.explanation: The post-hoc report lists only years of experience and education level.
flawedExample.why: The decisive feature is completely omitted — an incomplete attribution.

facets.name: Incomplete attribution
facets.example: A local attribution-based method lists only income and experience to justify the rejection, even though the model used zip code to reject an applicant.

facets.name: Inverse attribution
facets.example: A global attribution-based method reports that lower age increases credit risk, whereas the model's internal logic uses lower age to decrease risk.

facets.name: Ineffective counterfactual
facets.example: A counterfactual method suggests to switch employment status, but varying all employment status options yields the exact same model score.

facets.name: LLM rationalization
facets.example: An LLM-generated explanation for the rejection states: “Your loan has been rejected because our evaluation shows severe insolvency and a high probability of imminent default.” However, probing the model's chain of reasoning reveals that it did not read in the applicant's data but researched typical reasons for rejections.

lenses.footnote: An explanation is already unfaithful if it corresponds to a single facet. It can — but does not need to — correspond to multiple facets.
